summary: Pattern-seeking for 8–9 year-olds: children take repeated measurements of an object's motion under varied conditions (classically, how far a toy car rolls from different ramp heights), organise the readings into a table and graph, identify the relationship (e.g. 'the steeper the ramp, the further it rolls', for the heights tested), and then use that pattern to predict motion in an untested case — before testing the prediction. The pedagogically ideal vehicle is a real hands-on investigation where children do the measuring, repeat readings, and meet genuinely uncontrollable variables themselves; an on-screen ramp-and-car simulation is intended to rehearse the data→pattern→prediction reasoning as an alternative but does not build real-apparatus measurement craft. The core objective is that a prediction is an evidence-based inference anchored in collected data, not a guess, and that pattern-seeking is real science alongside the fair test.
misconceptions: Thinking one reading is enough — not repeating measurements, so noise is mistaken for pattern.
Believing only 'fair tests' produce trustworthy science, so pattern-seeking feels 'not real science' (AKSIS: fair tests dominate >50% of practical work).
Treating a prediction as a guess rather than an inference justified by the collected data/pattern.
Expecting an exact value rather than a trend-based prediction ('about this far / further than before').
Not separating the condition being changed from the quantity being measured when recording.
(Content) believing all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size or shape (Oak National Academy).

activities.title: Hands-on ramp-and-car pattern investigation
steps: Start from a 'big question': 'Does a steeper ramp make the car roll further?'
Set up real apparatus — a ramp you can prop at different heights, a toy car, a metre rule, and (optionally) a stopwatch.
Release the car from the SAME start point each time, raising the ramp in steps, and measure the distance it rolls for each height.

Take repeat readings (at least two or three) at each height, and record all readings systematically in a table that keeps the changed condition (ramp height) and the measured quantity (distance rolled) in separate labelled columns.
Plot the results on a graph (bar, line, or scatter as appropriate) so the trend across readings becomes visible.
Use 'what do you notice?' to state the relationship in your own words (e.g. 'for the heights we tried, the steeper the ramp, the further it rolls').

PREDICT, THEN TEST: for a ramp height you have NOT tried, use the pattern to predict the roll distance (best between your measured heights; if beyond them, only a little and with more caution), mark it, then run that height and compare the car's actual stop to your prediction.
Judge success by how close the actual distance is to the predicted trend, not by an exact hit, and raise a new 'big question' the enquiry suggests.
activities.insight: A pattern found across many readings can be used to make and justify a prediction about an untested, related case; a prediction grounded in your own data is an evidence-based inference, not a guess.

activities.title: On-screen ramp-lab simulation (data→pattern→prediction)
steps: Use a ramp-and-car sandbox: a slider sets ramp height; tap RELEASE and the car rolls while the distance is auto-measured.
Watch each run drop a point onto a growing table and scatter graph beside the track; after a few runs a trend becomes visible.
Deliberately repeat runs at the same height to see the slight scatter, so reliability is felt rather than assumed.

Take a PREDICT challenge: set the ramp to a height you haven't tried, mark where you think the car will stop on the track, then release and compare the car's actual stop to both your marker and the trend.

Notice the small run-to-run variation the simulation includes (e.g. a gentle random nudge standing in for real-world wobble), which is why repeat runs differ slightly and predictions are 'about this far' rather than exact.
activities.insight: The reasoning core of pattern-seeking — accumulate readings, spot the trend, predict an untested case, then check — can be rehearsed and made visible when live data capture links each run to a growing graph.

activities.title: Pattern-use consolidation questions
steps: Given a described or shown trend, predict the distance at a new ramp height (e.g. choose a value along a slider or number line consistent with the pattern).
Order a set of results by ramp height to see the trend as a sequence.
Choose which conclusion the data supports, rejecting an over-precise option that claims an exact value the data cannot justify.
Sort statements into 'pattern shown by the data' vs 'not supported by the data'.
activities.insight: Reading a trend and extrapolating a reasonable (not over-precise) prediction can be checked and reinforced once the investigate-measure-predict experience has been had.

activities.title: Finished-results graph with reveal (supporting scaffold)
steps: Study a finished results graph (ramp height vs distance rolled) and tap to reveal labels for axes, readings, and the trend.
Describe the relationship shown and point to where an untested height would fall on the trend.
activities.insight: A completed graph can help children read a trend and locate where a new case sits, as preparation or support for doing the full loop themselves.

checkQuestion: Here is a ramp you can prop at different heights, a toy car, and a metre ruler. Investigate how the ramp height changes how far the car rolls across the floor. Take the measurements you need, find the pattern, then use it to predict how far the car will roll from a height I choose that you haven't tried — and test your prediction.
checkAnswer: Releases the car from the same start point each time, raises the ramp in steps, measures the roll distance for each height (repeating readings), notices the pattern 'higher ramp -> further roll', predicts a new height's distance consistent with that trend (interpolating or extrapolating), then tests it by measuring — judging success by closeness to the prediction, not an exact hit.
